passage:
Wednesday, late
Diary, I did it. I told Arohi.
For weeks I've been waking at 4 and just lying there. School feels like wading through mud, and I stopped going to the terrace with the others. I kept telling everyone "just tired." Today Arohi (my cousin, the one who calls me "Hansu") stayed over, and while we were brushing our teeth she said, "You're not okay, na?" I nearly said "I'm fine." Then I started crying with toothpaste on my chin.
She didn't freak out. She sat on the edge of the bath and listened. She said, "Let's tell Mummy now. I'll come with you." I said yes.
Mummy turned off the TV and held my hand while I talked. She said it wasn't my fault, and that we'll talk to the school counsellor together.
I don't feel fixed. But I feel less alone than I have in a month.
Hansa

qa.a: Hansa told cousin Arohi, while they were brushing their teeth.

qa.q: What does "less alone than I have in a month" suggest about Hansa?
qa.a: Hansa had been carrying the low mood alone for weeks, and telling Arohi eased that loneliness even though the problem is not solved.

qa.q: Hansa nearly said "I'm fine" again. Why was saying yes to telling Mummy that same night an important choice?
qa.a: Arohi's support is real, but a parent can do more, and Mummy's calm answer led straight to a plan to see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: How might Arohi have been feeling when she asked "You're not okay, na?"
qa.a: She had probably noticed Hansa pulling away and was worried. Asking was a risk, and staying calm when Hansa cried shows she cared more about Hansa than about saying the perfect thing.

For three weeks Nkechi had eaten lunch alone in the library of her Dublin school, telling her mum she had "group projects." She had stopped drawing, even in art, the one class she used to love. On Thursday, when the bell rang, she stayed at her easel. Ms Hana, the art teacher, noticed the blank sheet.
"Everything all right?"
Nkechi almost said yes. Instead she said quietly, "Not really. I feel heavy all the time, and I can't face anyone at lunch anymore."
Ms Hana pulled up a stool and sat with her. "Thank you for telling me. You don't have to carry this by yourself." She listened while Nkechi explained about the friends who had drifted away. Then she said, "Let's go and see Mr Byrne, the school counsellor, together right now. And we'll ring your mum this afternoon, with you in the room." Nkechi nodded.

qa.q: What did Nkechi tell her mum she had at lunchtime?
qa.a: She told her mum she had "group projects."

qa.q: Why might Nkechi have almost said yes?
qa.a: She had been hiding it for weeks and may have feared being a bother or being judged, so saying yes felt easier than admitting how heavy things were.

qa.q: Which choice turned the afternoon around for Nkechi?
qa.a: Answering "Not really" instead of yes; that honest reply let Ms Hana sit with her and connect her to the counsellor and her mum the same day.

qa.q: How might Nkechi's mum feel when the call comes that afternoon?
qa.a: She may be worried and sad to hear about the lonely weeks, but glad Nkechi spoke up and that they can support her together.

grounding: A struggling teenager stops hiding and tells a trusted teacher, who listens and connects her to the counsellor and her mother that same day.

At the residential school in Shillong, evening study hour was nearly over when Rekha, fifteen, slid a folded note across the hostel common room to her cousin Charu. It said: "Can we talk? I'm not okay."
They sat on the back steps. Rekha's words came slowly. She hadn't been sleeping, she'd stopped calling home, and most nights she cried in the bathroom because she felt she didn't belong here. "I didn't want anyone to know," she said.
Charu squeezed her hand. "I'm really glad you told me. Let's tell Mrs Lyngdoh too, tonight."
Mrs Lyngdoh, the housemother, was still in her office. She put down her pen, listened to all of it and said, "Thank you for trusting us. This is not something you should hold alone." She rang Rekha's parents while the cousins sat beside her, and booked Rekha in with the school counsellor for the next morning.

qa.q: What did Rekha's note to Charu say?
qa.a: "Can we talk? I'm not okay."

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling that made her cry in the bathroom most nights?
qa.a: She felt she didn't belong at the school and was lonely and worn out, and she didn't want anyone to know.

qa.q: What did Charu choose to do after listening, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: Charu suggested telling Mrs Lyngdoh that same night, which brought in an adult who called Rekha's parents and arranged the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Rekha's parents feel after Mrs Lyngdoh's call?
qa.a: They would likely be worried to hear she had been struggling, but relieved that she reached out and that the school was already supporting her.

passage: Preeti, you asked how I got through Class 10 when things at home were bad. Okay. My parents were separating, the house was loud every night, and I stopped doing homework. I didn't tell anyone. I thought if I just kept quiet, it'd pass. Then my marks fell, and I felt worse. One day Anjali ma'am, our English teacher, asked me to stay after class. She said, "Payal, you've been very quiet. Is something going on?" And I don't know why, but I just told her. Everything. I cried in the staff room. She listened, then she took me to the school counsellor that same afternoon. The counsellor called my mother, gently. Things at home didn't get fixed right away. But I wasn't alone with it anymore. That's the part that saved me. Telling someone. So, Preeti, if you're carrying something, tell me. That's all.

Hrithik, come, put your phone down a minute. You've been quiet all week, and it reminds your old grandpa of something.

When I was fifteen, the year the mill shut and your great-grandfather lost his job, I stopped doing homework. I sat at the back. I told everyone at home I was fine, because they had enough troubles.

Our English teacher, Mrs D'Souza, kept me back one day. She didn't scold. She said, "Joseph, you used to write the best essays in this class. What's happening?" I meant to say nothing. Instead, the whole thing came out, the mill, the shouting at home, how I couldn't sleep.

She listened. She told me I wasn't the only one carrying things like that. That same day she spoke to my mother, gently, and after that she let me stay after school to study where it was quiet.

I've never forgotten it. So, Hrithik, is there someone you could tell?

The rain came down so hard the last bus from the cricket academy was forty minutes late. Karthik and Lalit sat under the tin shelter, bags between their knees.

"You've been off for weeks," Lalit said. "Missing nets, snapping at everyone."

Karthik stared at the puddles. He could say he was tired. Instead he said, "I'm not okay. Appa wants me to make the state team and top the class. I'm failing maths. I lie awake every night thinking I'm letting everyone down."

Lalit was quiet, then bumped his shoulder. "Man. Thanks for telling me. That's a lot."

"Don't tell anyone."

"I won't spread it. But you need a grown-up on your side. What about your amma? I'll come in with you when we get to yours."

The bus finally splashed in. At Karthik's gate, Lalit went inside with him. Amma looked up from the stove, saw their faces, turned it off and sat down to listen.

Damini had moved to Pune in June, and by September she still ate lunch alone. At home she said school was "good." At night she lay awake, feeling like a ghost in the corridors.
On Saturday, her cousin Vandana didi, who studied at a Pune college, came over for lunch. Afterwards, on the balcony, Vandana asked, "How's the new school, really?"
Damini opened her mouth to say "good." Then she stopped. "Honestly, didi, it's terrible. Nobody talks to me. I pretend to read in the library at lunch."
Vandana didn't laugh or give a lecture. She listened, then said, "That sounds so lonely. Thank you for telling me." That same evening, with Damini beside her, she told Damini's mother, gently, and they sat together to plan: a hobby club at school, and a chat with the class teacher on Monday.
Damini felt lighter than she had in months.

For two months after I missed selection for the state swimming team, I told everyone I was fine. I'm Harish, and I'm sixteen. I kept going to practice, but I felt heavy all the time. I stopped eating properly and lay awake replaying the race.
My cousin Nirmala akka, who is twenty-four and works in Chennai, came home for Pongal. On the second night, she found me on the terrace at midnight. "You haven't smiled once since I came," she said.
I almost said "tired." Instead I told her everything. The race, the heaviness, the not sleeping.
She didn't fix it. She just sat close and said, "I'm so glad you told me." Then, that same night, she woke my mother, and the three of us talked in the kitchen till two.
It didn't make it disappear. But hiding it had made everything heavier. Telling someone made it something we could carry together.
